passage:
Come, sit, Chinmay. You've been very quiet lately, so let me tell you about the year I turned twenty. I'm Thomas, and I don't tell this often.

That year a flood took the house and the shop in one night. We had done nothing wrong, and I was furious. For a month I said nothing to anyone. I went to church, I sang, I felt like a wall.

Then one night I stood alone in the empty pews and shouted at God. Every ugly thing I could think of.

Old Mrs. Pillai found me there. She didn't scold. She put the book of Psalms in my hands. "Half of it is people complaining to God," she said.

Neighbours brought rice and blankets for weeks. The anger didn't vanish, but it stopped turning to stone.

qa.q: What took the house and the shop in one night?
qa.a: A flood took the house and the shop in one night.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel in the first month, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Thomas was furious and shut down: no words to anyone and feeling like a wall, until the anger came out as shouting in the empty pews.

qa.q: What helped Thomas, and what could Chinmay take from it?
qa.a: Letting the anger be spoken, the Psalms and the neighbours' rice and blankets helped, so Chinmay could let anger speak and lean on people nearby instead of swallowing it.

qa.q: How does Mrs. Pillai see Thomas's shouting?
qa.a: Mrs. Pillai does not scold; by handing over the Psalms and saying half of it is complaining, she treats the protest as something faith can hold.

grounding: Thomas is angry at God for undeserved suffering, lets the anger speak, and is held by time, text and neighbours.

passage:
Jagdish: I skipped gurdwara again today
Manjula: you ok?
Jagdish: honestly no. I'm angry. at God. is that allowed
Jagdish: we did everything right. Papa did seva every Sunday for 20 yrs. and the fire took the whole shop anyway
Manjula: I think you're allowed to be angry
Jagdish: everyone at home keeps saying 'it's His will' and I just nod
Jagdish: inside I'm screaming
Manjula: my nani used to say even the prayers she learnt as a kid have lines that argue with God
Manjula: maybe you don't have to swallow it
Jagdish: I've been swallowing it for 3 weeks. now I just feel numb
Manjula: that's what scares me a bit. can you say it out loud to someone there? the granthi-ji you like?
Jagdish: maybe. he always has time after the evening prayer
Manjula: go tomorrow. and call me after
Jagdish: ok. thanks for not telling me to just have faith

qa.q: For how many years did Papa do seva every Sunday?
qa.a: Papa did seva every Sunday for 20 years.

qa.q: What is Jagdish feeling after three weeks of swallowing it?
qa.a: Jagdish feels angry at God and now numb after holding it in for three weeks.

qa.q: What does Manjula suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Saying the anger out loud to the granthi-ji Jagdish likes, because letting it speak within the community helps more than swallowing it.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's family see the fire?
qa.a: The family seems to find comfort in calling it God's will, which is why they keep saying so.

grounding: A chat shows anger at God after undeserved loss, and a friend encouraging Jagdish to let the anger speak and bring it to his faith community instead of going numb.

passage: After the flood took the family's cotton field and their only cow, Sonali stopped going to the Hanuman temple at the edge of her village in Vidarbha. Every evening her mother lit the lamp at home and folded her hands, and every evening Sonali left the room. Sonali had done nothing wrong, and neither had her parents. At the canal one evening, the priest's son Vijay, who had been at school with her, sat down nearby. 'You look like you want to throw stones at the temple bell.' 'I do,' Sonali said. 'We prayed. We fasted. And the river came anyway.' Vijay didn't argue. 'My father says the old women's songs at the temple are half complaints to God. Come on Tuesday when they sing. You don't have to pray. Just shout with them.' On Tuesday Sonali sat at the back of the temple courtyard. The songs were full of 'why'. She cried, for the first time since the flood.

qa.a: The flood took the family's cotton field and their only cow.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling toward the temple?
qa.a: Sonali felt angry at God, wanting to throw stones at the temple bell because the prayers had not helped.

qa.q: What did Vijay suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Joining the women's songs full of complaint on Tuesday, which let her anger speak inside the community instead of being bottled up.

qa.q: How does Sonali's mother seem to cope after the flood?
qa.a: Her mother keeps lighting the lamp and praying each evening, finding steadiness in her faith.

grounding: Shows anger at God after a flood the family did not deserve, and a friend guiding Sonali to let the protest speak within the community's songs.
